div.head: Introduction to Reading Notebook 07.01.04
div.p: Of all Marianne Moore’s reading notebooks, this one from 1923 may be the most closely linked to the simultaneous work she was drafting in a poetry notebook and it may itself most resemble the kinds of work she was doing in drafting poetry. Moore kept this 1923 Reading Notebook at the same time as she was working on the major poems at the beginning of her 1922-1930 poetry-drafting notebook. The confluence of interests in these notebooks is illuminating and there are numerous instances in which material quoted or paraphrased in this reading notebook migrates into her poetry drafts. In even more places, Moore takes notes on topics related to poems she is drafting without leaving evidence of any direct borrowing. It is also significant that Moore makes an extensive index of her reading in this notebook, including several cross-references—an experiment she repeats in 1924 when constructing her ironic, playful, and captivating index for Observations.

Several early pages of this 1923 reading notebook contain notes perhaps or definitely related to Moore’s late drafting of “Marriage.” According to notes provided by Patricia C. Willis, Moore began her poetry draft notebook with the earliest extant stages of thinking toward “Marriage,” around October 1922; she begins this reading notebook in January 1923 and she sent “Marriage” to Monroe Wheeler for publication in October of 1923 (the poem first appeared in Wheeler’s Maniken). This would indicate that Moore is taking notes in this reading notebook during most of the time that she is drafting “Marriage.” The most significant contribution to “Marriage” from this reading reveals that the oft-quoted line “The fact of woman / is not / ‘the sound of the flute / but very poison’” originates not with A. Mitram Rhibany, The Syrian Christ—as Moore indicates in her published “Notes” to the poem—but instead from a January 1923 article by Ananda K. M. Coomaraswamy, “Indian Art in Boston.” The internal quotation on flutes and poison has nothing to do with women but instead refers to Krishna playing a flute, and the text reads (as quoted by Moore): “This is not merely the sound of a flute, but very poison" (view p. 10v). It is Moore’s own imagination that combines this reflection on the gentle and “Divine Herdsman” relaxing at sunset with misogynistic reflections on women.

Early in 1923 Moore also takes notes on Lionel George’s “The Art of Courtship,” indicating that courtship requires “low cunning” and that “Such monsters must look after themselves in the lists of love.” Notes on a review of Stella Benson’s The Poor Man narrate a belligerent scene in which a woman stipulates to a man “Leave me alone” and after he continues to pursue her “she hit him on the Face” (view p. 12v). Such reading may contribute generally to the verbal insults traded by “He” and “She” in “Marriage” and to Eve’s stipulation there: “I should like to be alone.” A few months later, Moore quotes from a Leigh Hunt article “An Answer to the Question ‘What Is Poetry’” lines from Shakespeare’s Love’s Labour Lost that may be echoed in her “Marriage.” Hunt writes (as Moore quotes it), “This senior-junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid; / Regent of love-rimes, lord of folded arms, / The annointed sovereign of sighs & groans” (view p. 36v). In her own poem, Hymen is more mildly “unhelpful” and “‘a kind of overgrown cupid’,” and she ends this extended passage with the profound plea that “One must not call him ruffian / nor friction a calamity— / the fight to be affectionate: / ‘no truth can be fully known / until it has been tried / by the tooth of disputation.’” Moore borrows from what others are writing about conflict between the sexes but in her most famous poem on this topic she herself presents disputation as an inevitable fight ideally pushing toward truth and affection.

The poem “Mediaeval,” cited from an April 1923 Punch contributes phrases and lines to “Sea Unicorns and Land Unicorns” (first published in Moore’s December 1924 edition of Observations) and in June of 1923 she begins reading the first of a handful of sources contributing directly to “An Octopus,” also first appearing in the 1924 Observations. These notes contribute additional information to the sources Moore mentions in her own notes. For example, the line “glass that will bend” comes from an essay titled “Chance for Inventors”; in her published note, Moore mentions only Sir William Bell, the author of this list of what he perceives as needed inventions (view p. 29r)—although the rest of her unusually long note quotes verbatim from the list of inventions that she writes into her reading notebook. This frequently syndicated essay can now be found online in the MMDA under “Moore’s Sources”—along with other essays she cites, articles she annotates, or images she refers to, or draws from, in other notebooks.

These reading notes also make it clear how quickly Moore pulled at least some of her poems into final form after months of relatively chaotic drafting—as one can see from her poetry notebooks online. It could also be that Moore’s practice of eclectic reading and note taking in her reading notebooks influences in some way the apparently disorderly drafting of poems in her poetry notebooks, in which ideas or even lines eventually belonging to one poem are first presented on pages that also contain lines initially used in another poem.

In this notebook, Moore quotes a good deal of poetry—from children’s rhymes to poems by famous authors. Perhaps even more noteworthy is that she takes extensive notes on people writing about poetry: Sidney’s “The Defence of Poesy,” Shelley’s “A Defence of Poetry,” Robert Bridges’ “Poetic Diction in English,” and the Leigh Hunt essay previously mentioned on “What is Poetry”—interestingly the second half of the title but the only part Moore puts in large letters in her notes (view p. 36v). In this early stage of Moore’s career as a reviewer and essayist, she seems to be doing a lot of reading and thinking about the place of poetry in the world and how one might read, write, and judge it. From the Hunt essay, Moore quotes that “the quickest way of knowing bad poets from good” is the “perusal of the best poets w the greatest attention; and second, the cultivation of that love of truth & beauty which made them what they are. It is a good practice to read w pen in hand”—an admonition she has already followed for years!

Craftsmanship and creativity are also recurring topics in this notebook: from industrial design to folk arts, high literary art to children’s stories, antique furniture to imaginary inventions, Moore’s notes on these themes are wide-ranging. Reading the notebook as a whole situates Moore’s reading and thinking about the nature and practice of poetry among notes relating to other arts: about the ratio of plain to decorative elements in the industrial arts; the fabric, kinds of thread, and stitches used in embroidery; the compositional elements used by Chinese painters; the detailed lacquer carving techniques of Chinese furniture makers; the agrarian motifs of Indian artists; and so on. The Chinese lacquer notes are taken from the essay “Chinese Furniture” in a December 1922 supplement to the Spectator she apparently read in January 1923. “Bowls” (first published July 1923 in Secession 5), begins with a description of lawn bowls as involving “ancient punctilio / in the manner of Chinese lacquer carving, / layer after layer exposed by certainty of touch and unhurried incision / so that only so much color shall be revealed as is necessary to the picture” (NCP 60).White, Heather. Marianne Moore: New Collected Poems. NY: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2017. Hereafter abbreviated as NCP. While Moore does not mention this essay on furniture or quote from it directly, the comparison must be on her mind and she refers in her 1923 notes to the “consummate craftsmanship” and “amazing patience & skill” of the Chinese carvers.

Moore’s notes on craft also highlight the role of creativity in the making of new forms across media and genres, such as the previously mentioned list by Sir William Bell of inventions “the world needs” (view p. 29r), and her attention to Georg Brandes’ Creative Spirits of The Nineteenth Century (view p. 28v), or Thomas Hardy’s poem “An Ancient to Ancients” (view p. 117r). The cumulative effect of these assembled notes is that Moore may have been thinking about the craft of poetry as related to other artisan and artistic practices and traditions. In particular, it suggests that an exploration of generalized processes of making—of poesis—was stimulating to her own reflections on how and why poetry itself is made, and perhaps even to her own poetry-making. Moore insists in later years that she should not be called a “poet,” but perhaps she would call herself a crafts-person.

For the most part, the relation of poetry to other art practices is an idea only raised by the thematic patterns of Moore’s sources, that is, by her selections and the lines of interest these imply. At least once, however, the idea that poetry might best be understood through the study of other media and genres is articulated explicitly: as Moore notes, Bridges theorizes poetic diction through aspects of composition borrowed from theatre and painting. Surprisingly, this and other passages in the notebook reveal how the nature and quality of artistic materials—the basis on which the arts are typically distinguished from one another—are also salient to comparative conceptualizations of art. For instance, Moore’s recording of different kinds of vernacular in this notebook (and in several others)—from baseball commentary, to the language of advertisements, to the literary prose styles of Alice Meynell and the Forsyte Saga—implies that vernacular itself is a kind of raw material to be plied by the poet, not unlike silk, thread, lacquer, paint, wood, or glass.

Written in recto-verso format, this lovely, leather-bound notebook is written straight through, from start to finish, and includes reading notes exclusively. Unlike many others, it is not repurposed and may have been a gift to the poet. The notebook is small and Moore’s handwriting and page composition are neat and easy to read; special formatting occurs only when she transcribes a poem, indenting the lines, and in her final index. Likewise, the notebook contains only a few unusual abbreviations or markings: for example, Moore uses “hself” and “hs” (for himself and his) and she occasionally marks a line or phrase’s meter.

The index is an extremely significant feature of this notebook. Its alphabetic organization indicates that it was written once the notebook was full, rather than as each topic or entity occurred in Moore’s note taking. While others of Moore’s private reading notebooks also contain self-devised indexes, this one is unique due to the considerable overlap of its content with that of the index to Observations, suggesting strongly that this index may have been a model for the latter.See notebooks 07.01.02, 07.01.03, and 07.02.01. Indexical entries appearing in her 1923 reading notebook and in Observations include: “Adventures in Bolivia,” “Giraffe,” “Bacon, Francis,” “Chinese furniture,” “Craig E. G.,” “Glass that will bend,” “Hardy,” “Hunt,” “lacquer,” “Marriage,” “Octopus,” “Elephants,” “Shakespeare,” “Spenser,” and “Unicorn.” These and other entries from notebook 07.01.04 are a testament to the overlap between Moore's note-taking and her early stages of poetic composition, in which she recorded and connected themes, ideas, and phrases. It is all the more striking that in 1924 Moore shares a private bibliographic tool with readers of Observations, encouraging them to engage in a reading practice that mimicked both her note taking and her poetry drafting.

Among Moore’s notebooks, this one is a particular pleasure to read because its notes are so revelatory of her thinking at a time when she was astonishingly productive, writing many of her greatest poems. The notebook includes no drafting toward any poem but seems the indispensable companion to her drafting as she completed the poems and the organization of Observations.
